opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's actually one of the most valuable pieces of advice I got during my PhD. When I first interned at FAIR and worked with Kaiming, it went really well. We did ResNeXt together, and I learned an enormous amount. The natural thing would have been to just keep coming back, because it was comfortable, productive, and Kaiming is an amazing mentor.

But at some point he basically told me something like, "You've already learned what you can from working with me in this style. You should go out and see how other people do research." It wasn't him pushing me away. It was him being very generous and thinking about my long-term development rather than his own short-term productivity. Many advisors, if they have a good student, want to keep that student close. Kaiming was the opposite.

His point was that research taste and methodology are shaped by the environment you're in. If you only work with one person, even someone brilliant, you may end up as a slightly weaker copy of that person. To develop your own perspective, you need exposure to different ways of thinking: different labs, cultures, problem selection, and ways of balancing engineering against ideas.

So I took that seriously and went to other places for internships, including Google and DeepMind. Each place felt quite different. Some environments were more about scale and infrastructure, others more open-ended and exploratory. Seeing those contrasts helped me understand what I actually cared about and what kind of researcher I wanted to be.

Looking back, I think that advice reflects how Kaiming thinks about research generally. He's very principled and doesn't optimize for the obvious local maximum. In a way, telling me not to keep working with him was itself a kind of research lesson: don't get stuck in one comfortable basin, go explore. I've tried to pass that on to my own students too. I tell them it's fine, even good, to leave and learn from other people.

r001.rationale: The response attributes to Kaiming the advice to experience how other people do research and explains that different labs and environments broaden an intern’s perspective and learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's actually a story I think about a lot. I was a PhD student at UC San Diego, and I did my first internship with Kaiming at Microsoft Research Asia, and then later at Facebook AI Research. We worked really well together — ResNeXt came out of that period, and honestly it was one of the happiest, most productive times of my PhD. So naturally, when it came time to think about the next summer, my instinct was just to go back. Why change something that's working?

But Kaiming was the one who pushed back. He told me something like, "You already know how I think. You've seen how I do research. If you keep working with me, you're going to keep learning the same lessons." He felt very strongly that a PhD is the one period in your life where you have the freedom to be exposed to totally different styles of thinking, and that I shouldn't waste it by optimizing for comfort or for the next paper.

At the time, to be honest, I was a bit confused. He's my mentor, he's telling me to go work with someone else — it felt almost like he was pushing me away. But in hindsight, it was incredibly generous advice. He wasn't thinking about what was good for him or for our collaboration. He was thinking about what would make me a more independent researcher in ten years.

So I went to Google and worked with a different group, with people who approached problems in a very different way — more about scale, systems, different kinds of questions. And it was uncomfortable at first, but that discomfort is exactly what he wanted me to experience. I learned that there isn't one right way to do research, and I started forming my own taste, rather than just inheriting his.

I think that's one of the things that defines Kaiming as a mentor. He's very quiet, but he has this very clear idea that the goal is not to produce clones of himself. It's to help people find their own direction. And now that I have my own students at NYU, I try to give them the same advice — even when it feels a little against my own interests.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Kaiming encouraged exploring a different group and organization to experience different research styles and learn beyond the lessons already gained from him.
